title: Practical token economics — sales playbook & positioning
content:
Purpose:
Quick tactical reference for RD sales/GTM teams — explain why we price by tokens, how to map tokens to buyer outcomes, recommended tier architecture, and simple discount language + objection scripts for common pushbacks. This is intentionally pragmatic: copyable lines, worked examples, and competitor notes so reps can move faster in calls.

TL;DR (for quick use)
- Metric: Tokens map directly to units of model work (generation + embeddings). Tokens = predictable unit for usage-based economics across text and embeddings.
- Positioning headline: ‘Pay for what you consume, not for seats or fixed endpoints — tokens let you align spend to actual product usage while enabling predictable discounts for committed volume.’
- Core sales hooks: lower unit cost at scale, burst-friendly (no upfront infra), and compatible with Dedicated/Private for customers who want capacity + predictability.

Why token pricing — short scripts by buyer type
- Engineering/Platform buyer: “Tokens represent the raw compute work the model must do. Because they’re usage units our runtime optimizes, we can transparently show cost per response and tune batching/kv cache to meet latency and cost targets.”
- Product/PM: “Tokens let you tie feature usage (summaries, chat turns, embeddings per item) to economics — you can forecast costs by expected MAU and average tokens per user.”
- Finance/Procurement: “Tokens are a metered unit similar to API calls or compute hours — we offer commitment-backed discounts and predictable invoices; if you need a PO or reserved capacity, we support Dedicated contracts.”

Mapping tokens to concrete product metrics (cheat-sheet)
- Short chat message (1–30 tokens) — use for microinteractions
- Long chat turn or generated article (1k–10k tokens) — heavy generation
- Embedding per item (128–768 tokens depending on encoder) — embeddings billed per call
- Reranking / rerank pass — small token counts but high QPS; consider batch pricing logic
Example small-customer forecast (monthly):
- 200k chat turns, avg 120 tokens/turn => 24M tokens
- 50k embeddings, avg embed call = 256 tokens => 12.8M tokens
- Total = 36.8M tokens -> present as ~37M tokens when discussing tiers

Tier architecture (recommended canonical tiers) — language to use inverse to product pages
- Trial / Developer (Free tier): 0–5M tokens / month. Purpose: low-friction evaluation, encourage embedding experiments.
- Growth (self-serve): 5–50M tokens / month. Purpose: productization, PLG expansion. Signal: higher throughput and improved SLAs.
- Business (committed): 50–500M tokens / month. Purpose: predictable cost, volume discounts, basic enterprise features (SAML, longer retention in Console).
- Enterprise (dedicated/private): 500M+ tokens or reserved GPU pools. Purpose: SLAs, on-prem/VPC, custom pricing, P0 support, term commitments.
Notes on conversion/communication:
- Always translate token buckets into example feature consumption (e.g., ‘50M tokens covers approximately X monthly active users with Y average turn length’) — reps should carry 2–3 archetypes for quick math.
- Avoid decimal units in conversations with procurement; round to nearest million and present as ranges.

Discounting & commitment language (short phrases reps can use)
- Headline: “Volume commitments unlock predictable per-token pricing.”
- For self-serve upsell: “We apply automated volume discounts as you cross thresholds — no separate contract required for standard tiers.”
- For business contracts: “We’ll exchange a committed monthly (or annual) token volume for a tiered discount schedule and prioritized capacity. The discount reflects committed throughput and guarantees.”
- For Dedicated/Private: “Pricing is capacity-based plus a managed platform fee; discounts are applied based on term length and capacity commitment.”
Rules of thumb for discounting (internal guidance)
- Standard volume breakpoints: 50M, 200M, 1B tokens (example thresholds — finance will produce final bands).
- Max list discount observable without exec approval: 30% off list for committed annual deals. For Dedicated engagements discounting interacts with capacity pricing; route to AE lead.
- Don’t ladder discounts by feature — ladder by signed committed tokens or reserved capacity. Keep message simple: predictable commit => better unit price.

Objection handling (copyable scripts)
- “Tokens are confusing”: “Totally — think of tokens like API calls or compute hours. We can model your current workload from a 1–2 week sample and show expected monthly token consumption and cost so you can compare apples-to-apples.”
- “We don’t have stable usage to commit”: “Start with growth tier and switch to a committed plan once you see stable usage; we’ll provide price-protection for a limited window to smooth the transition.”
- “We want a per-seat or instance price”: “Seats are fine for tooling on top of models, but tokens align spend directly with model inference. If you need fixed pricing for budgeting, we offer Reserved (Dedicated) capacity with a fixed monthly rate.”
- “Embeddings cost too much / we have millions of vectors”: “We recommend a hybrid approach: reserve a moderate committed tier for baseline usage and use burstable hosted capacity for spikes; also run eval-based quantization suggestions from Redwood Optimize to reduce per-vector cost.”

Competitive talking points (short notes — avoid naming)
- Per-endpoint providers: may look simpler but often require per-model endpoints and don’t offer hybrid dedicated/private with the same API. Pitch: Redwood = single API + consistent rollout & routing across modes.
- Flat-seat inference vendors: predictable but inefficient for bursty workloads — tokens scale to your usage and lower cost when usage is spiky.
- Commodity cloud GPU providers: offer raw horsepower but don’t provide model/serving optimizations, prefix/KV caching, or token-aware batching that reduce unit cost.

Sales playbook snippets (copy/paste ready)
- Intro email line for a PM/eng lead: “Quick question — how do you currently budget for inference? We help teams move from guesswork to predictable unit economics via token-based metering and optional reserved capacity.”
- Demo framing: “We’ll show actual token consumption for a 10-minute run of your workload and simulate cost at 3 scale points: dev, growth, and enterprise.”
- Negotiation close line: “If you’re comfortable with a 12-month committed token volume, we can build a tiered discount that lowers your per-token price and adds capacity guarantees.”

Operational notes for Solution Engineers (what to bring to call)
- Sample 1–2 week trace of API calls and payload sizes.
- Quick calculator (spreadsheet) that maps actions -> tokens -> monthly spend.
- 2 example archetypes for customer verticals (e.g., support automation: 10k MAU, avg 80 tokens/turn; catalog enrichment: 200k embeddings/month).

Open questions / next steps (internal)
- Ask finance to finalize the canonical volume breakpoints and discount ceilings (blocked).
- Create a one-page visual token calculator for reps (TO DO: GTMP-781).
- Draft short FAQ page for help center that explains token math with 3 examples.

Appendix — Worked example (customer pitch)
- Profile: B2B search startup, 120k DAU, 1.2M queries/month.
- Assumptions: avg 40 tokens/query, plus embeddings for indexing 50k items (avg 256 tokens/embed).
- Monthly tokens: queries = 48M, embeddings = 12.8M, total ≈ 60.8M.
- Suggested package: Business tier (50–200M) with an initial 6-month commitment at a 15% discount; include 99.9% API SLA and basic SSO.

End — one-pager summary for reps:
- Use tokens as the canonical unit in every price conversation.
- Translate tokens to customer product metrics (MAU, requests, embeddings) on the call.
- Commitments buy predictability and discounts; Dedicated buys capacity + isolation.
- Keep discount conversation about committed volume, not feature bundling.

Document history: draft created by Maya Chen; collaborative input from SEs (Julian, Nora) and pricing (Ben).
